claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of high-entropy alloys is governed by repeated passive-oxide formation, disruption, and reformation.
Mechanical action breaks down the passive oxide film.
Film breakdown locally exposes a reactive alloy surface to the corrosive environment.
Subsequent oxidation partially restores the passive film.
CrMoNbWV is a high-entropy alloy suitable as the candidate system.
The initial HEA surface has an intact, protective passive oxide layer formed under static conditions.
Concurrent controlled sliding or oscillatory contact in an electrolyte induces tribo-corrosion.
Passive-film integrity and its cyclic disruption and regeneration at the wear track are the structural mediator.
Fresh metal exposed by mechanical film removal is more susceptible to corrosion.
Corrosion rapidly reforms a passive layer after mechanical removal.
Repeated film removal and repair control both wear rate and corrosion kinetics.
Relative to static corrosion, simultaneous tribo-corrosion produces greater total degradation.
Simultaneous tribo-corrosion produces higher localized corrosion rates than static corrosion.
Simultaneous tribo-corrosion produces enhanced wear damage relative to the static-corrosion baseline.
The surface degradation pattern should show periodic changes corresponding to film rupture and reformation.
The proposed mechanism applies where protective oxide passivation is the dominant corrosion-protection mechanism.
The prediction may fail for non-passivating alloys or when bulk deformation dominates wear.
The magnitude of enhancement depends on oxide-formation kinetics, wear-stress distribution, and alloy composition.
Identical-composition specimens under simultaneous tribo-corrosion and static corrosion provide a controlled comparison for the effect of mechanical action.
Absence of cyclic film disruption and regeneration, or statistically indistinguishable degradation rates between test and baseline, would falsify the hypothesis.
